paras: Phonics is how children learn to read and spell by matching the SOUNDS in spoken words (phonemes) to the letters or letter-groups that spell them (graphemes), then blending those sounds together, left to right, to read a whole word. Spelling is the same skill in reverse: breaking a spoken word into its sounds (segmenting) and writing the matching letters for each one.
It is called "synthetic" phonics because children build (synthesise) words from their smallest sound parts, rather than memorising whole words by shape or guessing from pictures.
Wren Phonics is a complete systematic synthetic phonics (SSP) programme, built to the Department for Education’s 16 core criteria for SSP programmes.

One programme runs from Reception through to Year 2: the same sound order, the same daily routine, and the same decodable books your child reads at school and brings home, so nothing your child meets at home contradicts what they are taught at school.
You may see your child's progress described using the familiar "Phase 1–6" labels. Wren Phonics groups these into three stages, with its own plain-English names:
"Introduction" (Phase 1, pre-school/early Reception): listening games, rhymes and sound-play — no letters yet. This is where children tune their ears in before the alphabetic code begins.

"Learning" (Phases 2–4, the bulk of Reception): the alphabetic code is taught directly, sound by sound, in a carefully sequenced order, alongside the first common "tricky" words that cannot yet be fully sounded out. Phase 4, in the summer of Reception, adds no new sounds: children read and spell words with two or three consonants together, like tent, stop and splash, saying every sound.

"School Readiness" (Phase 5 for most of Year 1, and Phase 6 — suffixes and prefixes — in the last half-term of Year 1, with Year 2 building on it): extra spellings for sounds already known, and the practice that leads up to and through the Phonics Screening Check.

Every sound is taught PURE: a quick, clipped sound for a "bouncy" letter like t, p or b (never "tuh", "puh", "buh"), and a sound you can hold for as long as you like for a "stretchy" letter like s, f or m (never "suh", "fuh", "muh"). Adding an extra vowel sound distorts blending, so if you are ever unsure how a sound should sound, ask your child’s teacher rather than guess.

sections.h: Why your child’s first reading book looks so simple
paras: Every decodable book your child brings home only uses sounds (and tricky words) they have ALREADY been taught, in that exact order — never a sound or word ahead of where they actually are. A tiny, simple-looking book at the very start of Reception is not a sign of anything being wrong; it is the whole method working exactly as intended. The books grow as the taught code grows.

Read with your child often, little and often. Give them time to sound a word out before helping; if they get stuck, prompt with "what’s the first sound?" rather than supplying the word. Praise the effort of sounding out, not just a correct answer. Let them re-read the same book more than once — that is exactly how fluent, confident reading is built, not a sign of being "stuck". A separate letter explains the two different kinds of book your child will bring home, and why they are used differently.
